extracted.intended_audience: practitioners/appellants and attorneys participating in USPTO disciplinary appeals and reconsideration proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules governing requests for reconsideration of USPTO Director final orders in Office disciplinary proceedings (who may file, timing, bases for relief, and related procedural limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration standard under 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: “No request for reconsideration or modification shall be granted unless the request is based on newly discovered evidence or error of law or fact, and the requestor must demonstrate that any newly discovered evidence could not have been discovered any earlier by due diligence.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the controlling regulatory standard the Director applies to requests for reconsideration or modification of a Director’s final order. The requester bears the burden to show either (a) newly discovered evidence (with due-diligence showing) or (b) clear error of law or fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limit to file a reconsideration request
rubrics_metrics.description: A single request for reconsideration or modification must be filed within twenty days from the date of entry of the decision. (See 37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c).)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests filed after this 20-day window are untimely and do not satisfy the regulatory filing requirement for reconsideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: New evidence must be truly newly discovered and discoverable only with due diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Any new evidence submitted must not have been available before the issuance of the final decision and the requester must demonstrate the evidence could not have been discovered earlier by due diligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (e.g., Boryan v. United States, Frederick S. Wyle P.C. v. Texaco) establish that evidence available prior to entry of judgment is not a basis for reconsideration. The requester must explain why the evidence was not previously available despite reasonable diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration is not a vehicle to relitigate or rehash prior arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsideration should not be used to rehash 'arguments previously presented' or to submit evidence that should have been previously submitted; mere disagreement with a final judgment is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court authorities (e.g., Hutchinson v. Staton; Arthur v. King; Wadley v. Park at Landmark) warn that requests repeating previously rejected claims or merely restating an appeal brief will be denied. The Director will compare the request against prior filings to detect repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy to Federal Rules of Civil Procedure (Rules 59/60) — narrow standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Federal Rules are not directly applicable, courts have used the standards for motions to alter or amend a judgment under Rules 59(e) and 60 as analogous guidance for § 11.56(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts treat such motions as narrow, limited to correcting new evidence or errors of law/fact. The USPTO has applied similar narrow review in prior proceedings (citing In re Faro, Piccone, Bang-er Shia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for reconsideration are extraordinary and rarely granted
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsideration is an 'extraordinary remedy reserved only for extraordinary circumstances.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities (e.g., Dowell v. State Farm; Projects Mgmt. Co. v. DynCorp) emphasize that relief is exceptional and should be used sparingly; mere dissatisfaction with the outcome is not enough.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effectiveness of Director’s reconsideration decision and stay requirement (§ 11.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reconsideration decision by the USPTO Director is 'effective on its date of entry' (37 C.F.R. § 11.56(c)). A stay of the decision can only be granted under 37 C.F.R. § 11.3, which permits suspension or waiver of non-statutory regulation requirements 'in an extraordinary situation, when justice requires.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reconsideration orders take effect immediately, requests to stay discipline pending reconsideration must independently satisfy the high § 11.3 standard (extraordinary circumstances). Disagreement with discipline is not sufficient to justify a stay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit on filings during appeals — permission required for additional briefs or motions (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(m))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO’s rules governing hearing appeals specify permitted pleadings and when they may be filed; 'Unless the USPTO Director permits, no further briefs or motions shall be filed.' (37 C.F.R. § 11.55(m)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing additional motions or briefs without leave (e.g., attaching a 'Motion to Dismiss' to a reply without authorization) is procedurally improper and subject to being stricken or denied. Briefing orders and prior orders governance control what may be filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of arguments not raised or developed on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments not raised or developed during the appeal are waived on reconsideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Smithkline Beecham Corp. v. Apotex and related authorities, the Director treats new arguments raised for the first time on reconsideration as forfeited unless they fall into exceptions (e.g., jurisdictional challenges).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO statutory authority over practitioner conduct (35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D), 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director and USPTO have statutory authority to regulate recognition and conduct of practitioners and to suspend or exclude persons from practice for incompetence, disreputability, or gross misconduct (35 U.S.C. § 32; 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This jurisdiction is broad and applies to practitioners engaged in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters; claims that § 32 applies only to patent matters are rejected based on the statutory scheme and precedent (Kroll v. Finnerty; Haley v. Lee; 37 C.F.R. § 11.19(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional challenges may be raised at any time
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject-matter jurisdiction arguments are not forfeited by failure to raise them earlier and may be raised at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing Cotton and related authorities, jurisdiction is a threshold issue that can be raised even on reconsideration, though a properly supported jurisdictional claim must still have merit to succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction analysis under 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanction determinations in disciplinary proceedings are made by considering the factors set forth in 37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ALJ applied § 11.54(b) factors in determining a 60-month suspension; while the Order does not enumerate those factors here, practitioners should expect sanction analysis to follow § 11.54(b)'s multi-factor approach and be prepared to address those factors at hearing and on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural consequence for improperly filed motions (striking/denying)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions filed without authority or leave (e.g., a Motion to Dismiss filed without permission and outside the permitted briefing) are improper and may be denied and stricken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond denying such motions on procedural grounds, the Director may also deny them on substantive grounds (waiver/forfeiture) if the issues were not timely and properly presented under the appeal/reconsideration process.
